request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Engineering maintenance technician, male, 4th year

[Earlier in the interview]

Interviewee: Since the new scheduling system went live, we can choose our shifts on our phones two weeks in advance, and if we want to swap a shift we don’t need to get the supervisor to sign off any more. We just tap it in the system with a colleague. Last month was my mum’s sixtieth birthday. I swapped three days of shifts in the system in advance, went back to my hometown and held a banquet with a few tables for her. All the relatives came, and my mum pulled me into loads of photos. When the system first went live there was a small problem: the handover time for the night shift was shown wrongly. I mentioned it to my supervisor, it was fixed the next day, and he let everyone know in the group chat. Old Zhou from our team says this system is much easier to use than the old spreadsheet. At least we don’t have to argue about the rota every month. Last year he even raised the scheduling issue at the all-staff meeting, and now it’s more or less been solved.

[Later in the interview]

Interviewer: Last week the general manager held a meeting to ask for everyone’s views on the new scheduling system. Did you raise anything?

Interviewee: No, I didn’t. Nobody in our team did. The system’s only been running for a month and everyone’s still getting used to it, so it’s a bit early to draw conclusions. Besides, the general manager was short of time that day. He had another meeting afterwards and only gave us twenty minutes in total. Several departments had to speak, and Engineering was last, so by the time it was our turn we’d already run over. The general manager looked at his watch several times, and in the end he said any remaining issues could be submitted in writing after the meeting. If there’s a problem, we can talk to our supervisor first, and the supervisor can pass it up the line. That’s more appropriate, and it doesn’t waste everyone’s time. Our supervisor’s quite easy to talk to as well. I think we should watch how it goes for a while longer. If anyone really has any ideas by then, it won’t be too late to find a chance to raise them.
